R04-C-01: Before the uniformed police forces that appeared in many large cities during the nineteenth century, the keeping of order was a patchwork. Night watchmen walked fixed rounds, parish constables served unpaid and often unwillingly, and private thief-takers recovered stolen goods for a fee, sometimes from the very thieves they claimed to pursue. What was new about the reformed police was not that they caught criminals more efficiently. It was the claim that a salaried, disciplined body of officers, visible on the street at all hours, could prevent offences from occurring at all. The patrol, rather than the arrest, was meant to be the core of the institution. This founding idea has an awkward property: its successes cannot be seen. A burglary that does not happen leaves no record, and a street that stays quiet because an officer passed through it twenty minutes earlier looks exactly like a street that would have stayed quiet anyway. The arrest, by contrast, is countable. It produces a name, a charge and a figure that can be reported upward and compared from one year to the next. Over time, institutions tend to drift toward what they can count, and police forces have been no exception. Officers come to be judged by how many people they detain, and the quiet beat, which was supposed to be the whole point, comes to look like idleness. It would be too simple to conclude that the preventive ideal was therefore an illusion. Critics sometimes point out that putting more officers on the street does not reliably reduce recorded crime, and they are right to be sceptical of large claims about deterrence. But the patrol was never only about deterrence. A visible and predictable presence tells residents that someone is responsible for the shared space of the street, and that sense of being looked after shapes whether people walk out at night, whether they report what they see, and whether they regard the police as theirs or as an occupying force. These effects are as hard to count as the burglary that did not happen, but they are not imaginary. The deeper lesson concerns what happens when a public institution is measured by its most legible output rather than by its purpose. A force that rewards arrests will produce arrests, and it may do so in ways that erode the trust on which prevention depends. Recovering the original idea does not mean abandoning measurement; it means admitting that some of the most important things a police force does will show up, if at all, only as an absence.
R04-C-02: We tend to think of the passport as a document that lets people travel. It is the thing we pack and check twice before leaving for the airport, and losing it abroad feels like being stranded. Yet the history of the passport suggests that its first purpose was not to open borders but to give states a means of closing them selectively. A document that certifies who you are, and which state answers for you, is above all a tool for deciding who may enter, who may leave, and who may be turned back. For much of the nineteenth century, a traveller could cross many European frontiers without being asked for papers at all. Controls existed, but they were patchy, and in several countries they were relaxed as railways made movement faster and cheaper. The First World War changed this. Governments anxious about spies, deserters and the flight of men of fighting age began demanding documents at every crossing, and when the war ended the requirement was not withdrawn. What had been introduced as an emergency measure became the ordinary condition of international travel, and the expectation that every person should belong to exactly one state, and carry proof of it, hardened into common sense. Few people now remember that it was ever otherwise. None of this makes the passport simply an instrument of control. For the person who holds it, it is also a claim on protection: it entitles the bearer to return home and to seek help from the officials of the issuing state when abroad. The predicament of stateless people, who have no government willing to vouch for them, shows how much that claim is worth. Without it, a person can be refused entry everywhere and expelled from wherever he happens to be. The more uncomfortable point is that the protection is unevenly distributed. Two travellers standing in the same queue may carry documents of identical design and very different power, one admitting its holder to most of the world without a visa, the other inviting suspicion at every desk. What the passport records, then, is not only identity but rank in an order of states, an accident of birth that the individual did little to earn and can rarely change. Nor is that rank settled by anything the traveller does at the desk; it is negotiated between governments, through visa agreements and reciprocal arrangements, long before any individual reaches the frontier. To call the document a passport to freedom is to describe the experience of those whose papers happen to work.
R04-C-03: Public debate about bureaucracy tends to oscillate between two complaints. One is that officials are rigid, applying rules mechanically to people whose circumstances the rules never anticipated. The other is that officials are arbitrary, treating similar applicants differently according to mood, prejudice or the length of the queue. The usual remedy for the second complaint is more rules: tighter eligibility criteria, standard forms, checklists that leave nothing to judgement. Each new scandal of favouritism produces another layer of instructions, and the layers accumulate. The remedy is seldom questioned, because it seems obvious that a rule applied uniformly is fairer than a person deciding as he pleases. What this remedy overlooks is that the officials who deal directly with the public, the benefits clerk, the housing inspector, the teacher deciding which pupil needs extra help, cannot stop exercising judgement however detailed their instructions become. A rule says that an applicant must provide proof of address; it does not say how hard the clerk should look for an acceptable document when the applicant has been living with relatives. Moreover, such officials almost always have more cases than time. They must decide whose file to open first, whose story to probe and whose to accept, and these decisions shape outcomes as surely as any formal ruling. When rules are tightened, judgement does not disappear. It retreats into these less visible choices, where it is harder to observe and correct. This is not to romanticise frontline discretion. The same latitude that allows a sympathetic clerk to find a way through for a desperate family allows an unsympathetic one to find reasons for delay, and there is ample reason to think that such latitude is not exercised evenly across applicants of different backgrounds. The case for discretion is not that officials can be trusted. It is that the choice is not between discretion and its absence, but between discretion that is acknowledged and discretion that is driven underground. Discretion of the first kind can be examined and improved; discretion of the second kind can only be suspected. Seen this way, the task of administrative reform changes. Instead of writing rules ever more finely in the hope of closing every gap, an agency might record the informal decisions its staff actually make, review samples of cases to see how similar applicants fare, and give officials explicit guidance on the purposes their judgement should serve. None of these steps would remove judgement from the counter; they would make it something an agency can see, discuss and, where necessary, correct. Such measures concede what the rule-writer prefers to deny: that every system of rules ends, at its edges, in someone deciding.
R04-C-04: Discussions of nationality law often begin from a tidy contrast. Under the principle of soil, a child born within the territory of a state becomes its citizen; under the principle of descent, citizenship passes from parent to child wherever the child is born. The first is commonly described as civic and open, since it admits anyone born on the land regardless of ancestry; the second as ethnic and closed, since it ties membership to bloodline. The contrast is useful as a first approximation, but as a guide to which societies are more welcoming it is close to misleading. Consider why states adopted the soil rule in the first place. Where governments needed to populate large territories and to secure soldiers and taxpayers, it was convenient to claim the children of newcomers automatically, whatever their parents' wishes or origins. The rule expressed less a generous conception of belonging than an interest in numbers. Conversely, the descent rule has served countries with large populations abroad, allowing the children of emigrants to retain a connection to a homeland they may visit only occasionally. Neither motive is obviously more liberal than the other, and the same rule can serve quite different ends depending on who adopts it and why. More importantly, the rule that governs birth is only one part of a citizenship regime, and often not the part that matters most. A state that follows the descent principle but allows long-term residents to naturalise after a few years, and extends citizenship to children who have grown up and been schooled in the country, may be far easier to join than a state that follows the soil principle but makes naturalisation slow, costly and uncertain for adults. The second state includes every child born on its territory and keeps their parents waiting at the door indefinitely. A single household may then contain citizens and foreigners under one roof, divided by nothing more than the place where each member happened to be born. None of this means the choice of birth rule is unimportant. The soil principle does guarantee something valuable: no one born in the territory can be left, by the mere fact of birth, a permanent outsider in the only country he has known, and states without it have sometimes produced generations of residents with no secure status. But that guarantee is better understood as one protection among several than as the defining mark of an open society. The question worth asking of any nationality law is not which principle it starts from, but how readily it turns people who have made their lives in a country into its members.
R04-C-05: There is an old argument, revived by students of public finance, that the way a state raises its money shapes the kind of state it becomes. A government that depends on taxing its own population must, to some degree, negotiate with that population. It needs to know who earns what and where they live; it needs officials who can assess, collect and keep accounts; and it needs taxpayers who will comply without being coerced at every turn. Each of these needs creates leverage for the governed. Those who pay can demand to know how their money is spent, and rulers who want a steady revenue have reason to listen. A government that draws most of its income from a single lucrative resource, such as oil or minerals sold abroad, faces no comparable pressure. Its revenue arrives through a handful of contracts with foreign buyers and requires little cooperation from ordinary citizens. It has no need to build an apparatus that knows the population in detail, and no need to trade services or a voice in decisions for compliance. Proponents of the argument suggest that such states can afford to be both unresponsive and administratively thin, buying acquiescence with subsidies and public employment rather than earning consent through bargaining. Stated baldly, the thesis is too mechanical. Taxation has often been extracted by force rather than negotiated, and many heavily taxed populations have obtained neither representation nor accountability in return. Nor are all resource-rich states alike: where competent institutions and habits of public scrutiny were established before a windfall arrived, the revenue has sometimes been managed with considerable openness. The sequence appears to matter as much as the source. A resource boom that lands on a weak state may keep it weak; one that lands on a state already accustomed to accounting for itself need not. What survives these qualifications is a narrower but sturdier claim. The point is not that taxes make governments good or that resource revenue makes them bad, but that accountability tends to grow where rulers need something from the ruled that cannot simply be seized. Taxation is one common source of that need, perhaps historically the most important, but it is the dependence, not the tax form as such, that does the work. A reform that raised more revenue from citizens without increasing what citizens could demand in return would therefore miss the point entirely, and might even entrench the habits of command it was meant to cure. Equally, a resource-rich government that chose to make itself dependent on its citizens, by funding services through broad taxes and setting its windfall aside, would be doing something more significant than balancing its books.
R04-C-06: Almost every modern constitution makes room for its own partial suspension. In a war, an epidemic or a sudden collapse of public order, the executive may be permitted to rule by decree, restrict movement or detain people without the usual procedures, on the understanding that these powers serve to preserve the constitutional order rather than to replace it. The logic is respectable. A constitution that made no provision for emergencies would not prevent governments from acting in a crisis; it would simply ensure that they acted outside the law, improvising powers with no defined limits and no defined end. The danger that emergency provisions are usually designed to guard against is the dramatic one: a leader who declares a crisis in order to abolish the constitution altogether. That danger is real but comparatively rare. The more common pattern is quieter. An emergency is declared for a genuine reason, and then renewed, and renewed again, because the threat has not entirely disappeared and no official wants to be blamed if it returns. Measures adopted as exceptions are gradually written into ordinary statutes, where they no longer need renewal at all. And each emergency lowers the threshold for the next, since officials and citizens alike grow accustomed to powers that once seemed extraordinary. The standard remedy is the sunset clause, which makes emergency powers lapse after a fixed period unless they are renewed. Sunset clauses are better than nothing, but they tend to turn renewal into a formality, a vote taken under the shadow of the original fear by legislators who see little to gain from being the ones who let the powers lapse. What matters is not whether powers expire but how hard it is to extend them. A more demanding design would require larger majorities for each successive renewal, so that a measure which commanded a bare majority at the outset needed broad agreement to survive a year later, and it would oblige the government to state publicly, each time, why ordinary law is still inadequate to the threat. Such designs would not prevent a determined government from abusing emergency powers, and no constitutional text can do that alone; courts, a free press and an opposition willing to make itself unpopular all have parts to play. The purpose of the design is more modest: to make normalisation visible and expensive, so that an exception which has outlasted its reasons must be defended openly as a permanent change rather than slipping into permanence unnoticed. A government that genuinely needs lasting powers can still obtain them, but only by persuading a broad majority that the change should be lasting. The test of an emergency regime is less whether it can survive a coup than whether it can end.
R04-C-07: Few political ideals are invoked as often, or defined as loosely, as the rule of law. In one usage it names a set of formal properties of a legal order: laws should be general rather than aimed at particular persons, public rather than secret, prospective rather than retroactive, clear enough to be followed, stable enough to be relied on, and applied by courts that are independent of those who hold power. In another usage the phrase stands for a much larger package. A state governed by the rule of law, on this richer view, is one that also protects fundamental rights, holds free elections and distributes its burdens fairly. Whatever is admirable in a constitutional democracy tends to be gathered under the same heading. The richer view has an obvious appeal. It seems perverse to praise a legal order for its clarity and consistency while it applies clear and consistent laws that strip a minority of its property or bar it from public life. Yet the inclusive definition carries a cost that its defenders seldom count. If the rule of law means everything good about a political system, the phrase ceases to pick out anything in particular. We lose the ability to say, of one regime, that its laws are cruel but at least public and predictable, or of another that it has excellent statutes on paper which officials ignore whenever it suits them. These are different failings, calling for different remedies, and a vocabulary that cannot separate them is a poorer instrument for judging governments, not a more generous one. The formal conception, moreover, is not as morally empty as its critics allege. A law that is public and prospective allows people to know in advance what will be required of them and to arrange their lives around it; a law applied by independent courts constrains the officials who administer it as well as the citizens who are subject to it. These are real goods even when the content of the law is objectionable, because they leave the governed some room to anticipate, avoid and contest what is done to them. It is also worth noticing that governments bent on oppression rarely find formal legality congenial. They tend to prefer secret directives, retroactive offences, vague charges that can be stretched to fit any critic, and enforcement that falls on enemies and spares friends. The formal requirements, in other words, get in the way of a great deal of injustice, even if they forbid none of it outright. This last point should not be pressed too far. The tendency of formality to obstruct oppression is a matter of experience, not of logic, and experience includes regimes that pursued grave injustice through meticulously drafted, publicly promulgated and impartially enforced laws. A defender of the thin conception must concede that legality of this kind is compatible with deep wrong, and that its tendency to discourage abuse is a probability rather than a guarantee. What can be claimed is narrower: that formal legality is one distinct virtue a legal order may have or lack, that its absence makes most other wrongs easier to commit, and that we see it most clearly when we refuse to let it stand for every other virtue at once. Questions about whether the laws are just, whether the rulers were chosen freely and whether the burdens are fairly shared remain, on this view, as urgent as ever; they are simply different questions, and they deserve to be asked in their own terms.
R04-C-08: Every entrenched constitution invites an awkward question. If a majority of citizens today wishes to change some arrangement, why should it be prevented from doing so by rules that were drafted generations ago by people who are now dead, and who could not have imagined the conditions under which their successors live? A requirement that amendments win two-thirds of the legislature, or the approval of most regions, looks from this angle like a device for letting the past outvote the present. The objection has a democratic edge that is hard to dismiss: it asks by what right one generation sets the terms on which another must govern itself. Nor is it answered by praising the wisdom of the framers, since wisdom about one century is no warrant for authority over the next. The most familiar answer appeals to self-binding. Just as a sailor who knows he will be tempted by a dangerous song may order his crew to tie him to the mast and ignore his later pleas, a people may bind itself in a calm moment against the passions it expects to feel in an agitated one. Entrenchment, on this account, is not the past overruling the present but the present protecting itself from its own worst impulses. The image is attractive, but it does not fit the case. The sailor binds himself, and the man who later strains at the ropes is the same man who gave the order. A constitution binds people who were not present when it was adopted and who gave no order at all. To call this self-binding is to assume precisely the continuity of the collective self that the objection calls into question. A better defence starts from a different picture of what entrenchment does. Amendment rules do not, in practice, pit the living against the dead, because the dead cast no votes. What such rules do is set the terms on which living citizens must settle disagreements among themselves. When an amendment fails for want of a supermajority, it is defeated not by its framers but by a present minority large enough to block it. The requirement thus protects groups that might otherwise be outvoted on matters basic to their standing, and it encourages proposals that can attract support beyond a single faction. The protection is not merely theoretical: a group that knows it can block changes to its basic standing has less reason to fear the ordinary swings of electoral fortune, and more reason to accept defeat on everything else. Seen this way, the hand that restrains the majority is a living hand, and the real question is whether present minorities deserve such a veto, not whether the past deserves obedience. This reframing does not make the original worry vanish. It succeeds only where amendment is demanding but genuinely possible. A constitution whose amendment procedure is so onerous that no change has been achieved in living memory, or which declares certain provisions unamendable altogether, really does impose the judgement of its authors on everyone who comes after; there, no present coalition, however broad, can alter the text. The objection from the dead hand is therefore best understood not as a refutation of entrenchment as such but as a warning about its extremes. Between a constitution that any passing majority may rewrite and one that no one can, the useful argument concerns how much agreement change should require, and that is a question each generation is entitled to keep asking.
